title: What an archive should keep
bodyMd:
Original paired historical-method commentaries.

Passage 1

A municipal archive cannot keep every paper that passes through every office. Selection is unavoidable, and a transparent policy is preferable to a series of quiet accidents. Records of major decisions should take priority because they let future readers determine who exercised authority and on what stated grounds. Routine duplicates and obsolete supply forms may be discarded under a published schedule. Staff should document those choices, including the categories of material not retained. An archive is necessarily incomplete, but it can be candid about the principles that shaped its incompleteness.

Passage 2

Formal decisions are essential records, but their neat language often conceals the negotiations through which policy takes effect. The everyday complaint, an informal reminder, or a repeatedly corrected application can reveal how a rule was experienced by people subject to it. No archive can preserve everything, and I do not propose that it should. I propose that selection policies reserve space for samples of ordinary transactions, chosen with clear methods. Otherwise future historians may find ample evidence of what the city announced and little evidence of what it actually did in daily encounters.
